cosing_function: Antioxidant; Emollient; Skin conditioning (reported via secondary ingredient databases; not independently confirmed via direct CosIng search this pass)
brief_description: Plant-derived (Psoralea corylifolia seed) meroterpenoid marketed as a gentler alternative to retinol. The key head-to-head RCT (Dhaliwal et al., Br J Dermatol 2019) found 0.5% bakuchiol twice-daily produced statistically comparable improvement in wrinkles and hyperpigmentation to 0.5% retinol every day/every-other-day over 12 weeks, with significantly LESS scaling and stinging reported in the bakuchiol arm. It appears to upregulate similar collagen genes (COL1A1/COL3A1) and downregulate MMPs, but through a different mechanism than direct retinoic-acid-receptor binding -- so it is a reasonable retinoid-intolerant substitute, not a proven pharmacological equivalent.

As a whole-plant extract it is not a single defined chemical (see pubchem_safety.csv note), so composition and potency vary by supplier and extraction method.

brief_description: Salicylate-based UVB chemical filter (peak ~306nm) also used as a solvent that helps dissolve less-soluble UV filters into a formula; not photostable on its own. Permitted to 15% in the US and 10% in the EU. SCCS review has flagged possible endocrine-disrupting activity as an open question, and the EU is re-assessing its concentration limits.

cosing_function: Light stabilizer; UV absorber; UV filter
common_synonyms: Ethylhexyl Methoxycinnamate; Octyl Methoxycinnamate; OMC; EHMC
brief_description: UVB-only chemical filter (peak absorption ~310nm); one of the most widely used sunscreen actives globally. US max 7.5%; the EU's SCCS concluded in 2025 that EHMC is safe as a UV filter up to 10% including in children. Frequently combined with UVA filters like Avobenzone for broad-spectrum coverage.

cosing_function: Light stabilizer; UV absorber; UV filter
brief_description: Oil-soluble UVB/short-UVA chemical filter (US max 10%) valued mainly as a photostabilizer for Avobenzone (raises its photostability from roughly 23% to 90% remaining after UV exposure); also used at low levels (0.2-0.5%) as a non-sunscreen light stabilizer in nail products. Long believed non-sensitizing, but recent dermatology literature documents a rising rate of contact and photocontact allergy, some cross-reacting with ketoprofen/benzophenone-3.

Inhalable powder/nano forms carry a separate GHS respiratory and carcinogenicity caution that applies to loose powder or spray products, not standard cream-based topical sunscreen.
